en: The Sutra on the Merits of the Bhikṣu Śākya, translated by the Śramaṇa Faju of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time...
He was accompanied by twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus and ten thousand bodhisattvas.
At that time, in the kingdom of Suyā, there was a poor man who worked as a hired barber for children; those whose heads he shaved all made an agreement with him:
"When the wheat is ripe, we shall each hire you for one *shǔ* of wheat."
Not long after he had departed, he encountered an old friend on the road who took him back with him.
Seeking barley so as to brew wine for his guest,
he searched everywhere, but no one returned any barley.
Thereupon, he gave rise to a mind of malice and said:
"May I, after the end of my life, become a great divine dragon and submerge this kingdom.
Later, when his life ended, his spirit was reborn as a dragon; for many years thereafter, wind and rain fell out of season within that country, and the five grains were ruined.
The Buddha, mindful that the people of this country were suffering from famine, immediately dispatched the bhikṣu Śākya to go and transform them.
When the dragon saw the bhikṣu approaching, he conceived an evil intent, wishing to destroy the kingdom and kill the bhikṣu Śākya.
Śarabha then miraculously transformed his almsbowl so that it covered an entire kingdom.
The dragon sent down rain, believing the country had already been submerged.
By means of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the bhikṣu caused the dragon to see that the people remained peaceful and secure as before.
The dragon, reviving his wrathful intent, brought down a snowfall; the bhikṣu received it with his alms-bowl.
When the snow reached its peak, the bhikṣu swept it away with his hand, piling it up in one place like a mountain.
The bhikṣu then entered the dragon’s chamber; as soon as he did so, the dragon came out, and when the bhikṣu emerged, the dragon went back in.
When the bhikṣu re-entered, the dragon re-emerged.
This continued for many such cycles until the dragon grew weary and desisted, whereupon it knelt upright and asked:
"What deity are you that you trouble me so?
The bhikṣu replied,
"I am a disciple of the Buddha."
The nāga said,
"I wish to take refuge in you.
The bhikṣu replied:
"I have a Great Master, the Buddha, who is most honored in the three realms; you should take refuge in him yourself.
The dragon asked, "Where is the Buddha?"
He replied, "The Buddha is in Śrāvastī. The nāga said:
"Please drive this practitioner away.
The bhikṣu said, "If you wish to leave, that is well!"
He then placed the dragon inside a chest.
When the people saw the bhikṣu take the dragon in such a manner, they were all filled with joy and asked,
"What kind of great deity is this practitioner who has subdued the calamity of our kingdom?"
He replied, “I am a disciple of the Buddha. The people asked:
"Can the Buddha be seen? He replied,
"If you wish to see the Buddha, wait for my return."

At that time, as the sun was approaching midday, he encountered people on his almsround. Some people gave him rice, while others gave him wine. The bhikṣu accepted and ate and drank it, becoming intoxicated with wine; he then lay down beneath a tree, where his alms bowl and his kāṣāya robe were each lying in a separate place.
At that time, the Buddha smiled, and light of five colors issued forth. Ānanda adjusted his robes, pressed his palms together, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha does not smile without cause; this smile must surely have a specific meaning!"
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
“Do you see the bhikṣu Śākya? Ānanda replied:
"I have not seen him.
The Buddha said,
"He is now lying drunk beneath that tree."
At that time, twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus and ten thousand bodhisattvas said to one another:
"The bhikṣu Śāgha has already attained arhatship; why does he still lie down drunk?"
The Buddha, knowing that the minds of those people harbored doubts, thereupon explained four matters:
"First, an Arhat cannot know [these things] unless he is in samādhi;
second, he cannot manifest supernormal powers (ṛddhipāda) at will."
Third, one must not forcibly urge others to go on almsround;
fourth, there are still insects within one's body.
For these four matters, the Arhat falls short of the Buddha.
At that time, ten thousand bodhisattvas all turned their minds and desired to go toward the arhats.
The Buddha dispatched Maudgalyāyana to the place of the bhikṣu Śākha, commanding him to bring the nāga under control.

The dragon prostrated itself before the Buddha with its head and face, and the Buddha then explained for it the origins and details of its past lives. The dragon’s mind was immediately enlightened; it received the five precepts, practiced the ten wholesome deeds, and attained the stage of Srotāpanna. It then paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
At that time, the Buddha spoke of the subtle and wondrous merits of the bhikṣu Śagha.
Ānanda joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The bhikṣu Śagha was drunk and lying prostrate from drinking wine; yet the Buddha speaks of his merits as being so subtle and wondrous?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Arhats no longer experience hunger or thirst; for three reasons, they manifest as being drunk and lying down.
First, the Buddha wishes to open and transform the minds of bodhisattvas."
Second, he did not wish to oppose the intentions of those who offered alms;
third, he feared that his disciples who had not yet attained the Way might lose themselves through excessive drinking.
By restraining them with these ultimate precepts, even though the Śākya bhikṣu drank wine, he remained sober.
When the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly of disciples heard the Buddha speak these words, they all rose, adjusted their robes, and paid homage to the Buddha.
The bhikṣu Śagha then stepped forward, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The King of Suyavya and his people wish to see [the Buddha]."
The Buddha accepted this by remaining silent.
The bhikṣu Śagha, having received the Buddha’s instruction, returned to the kingdom of Suyavya in the time it takes to snap one's fingers.
Upon seeing the bhikṣu, the king and the people were all filled with joy; some prostrated themselves, some knelt, while others simply joined their palms in reverence.
The bhikṣu Śagha announced:
"The Buddha shall arrive tomorrow.
Upon hearing that the Buddha was coming, the king was filled with great joy and anticipation; he swept and sprinkled the four crossroads and extensively prepared canopies and curtains.

On the following day, the Buddha, together with twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, traveled through the air in advance; beneath each of them were natural lotus flowers that arose spontaneously to receive his feet.

The king, along with his ministers and subjects, all took flowers and incense and went out of the city to welcome the Buddha. Prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, they bowed their heads in salutation.

When the Buddha and the bhikṣus arrived at the palace, there spontaneously appeared lion thrones spread with fine carpets and adorned with canopies of the seven precious gems and interwoven five-colored silks; the king prepared offerings, personally serving them with his own hands.
When the meal was finished, water for washing was served, and a prayer of aspiration was recited.

The Buddha then explained the origins and history of the dragon to the king and the people; their minds were awakened, and they immediately received the five precepts and practiced the ten wholesome deeds. Among them, those who attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, or *arhat* were beyond counting.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the fourfold assembly of disciples, along with the devas, nāgas, and spirits, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
Thus ends the *Sutra on the Merits of the Bhikṣu Śākya*.
